question.knowledge_point: Finding the Second Derivative of a Parametric Curve Given the First Derivative
question.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x={t}^{2}-1,\,y={e}^{-4t}.$ Given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2{e}^{-4t}}{t},$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2{e}^{-4t}}{t},$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}({t}^{2}-1)=2t
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{-2{e}^{-4t}}{t})}{2t} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{8t{e}^{-4t}+2{e}^{-4t}}{{t}^{2}})}{2t} \\  & =\frac{8t{e}^{-4t}+2{e}^{-4t}}{2{t}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-4t}(4t+1)}{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=\frac{1}{{t}^{3}},\,y=\frac{3}{t}.$ Given that $\frac{dy}{dx}={t}^{2},$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}={t}^{2},$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{1}{{t}^{3}})=-\frac{3}{{t}^{4}}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}({t}^{2})}{(-\frac{3}{{t}^{4}})} \\  & =\frac{2t}{(-\frac{3}{{t}^{4}})} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-3.$ Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,{y}^{′}(t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}=-\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t).
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t))}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-\frac{2{sec}^{2}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-{sec}^{3}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=2{e}^{3t},\,y=3{e}^{t+2}-5$ where $t$ is a real number. Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=6{e}^{3t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{e}^{t+2}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3{e}^{t+2}}{6{e}^{3t}}=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2-2t}.
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2-2t})}{6{e}^{3t}} \\  & =\frac{-{e}^{2-2t}}{6{e}^{3t}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}{e}^{2-5t}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Parametric Curve at a Given Point
question.problem: A curve has parametric equations $x=\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}-2,\,y={t}^{7}+2.$ Given that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=7{t}^{2},$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ at the point where $t=2.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=7{t}^{2},$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}-2)={t}^{4}.
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(7{t}^{2})}{{t}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{14t}{{t}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{14}{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate at $t=2,$ and we get

$$
{\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}|}_{t=2}=\frac{14}{(2)^{3}}=\frac{14}{8}=\frac{7}{4}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Parametric Curve at a Given Point
question.problem: A curve has parametric equations $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).$ Given that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cot}⁡(2t),$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{12}.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cot}⁡(2t),$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cot}⁡(2t))}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)} \\  & =\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡(2t)}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{csc}^{3}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate at $t=\frac{\pi }{12},$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}{|}_{t=\pi /12} & =-\frac{1}{4}{csc}^{3}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{12}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4{sin}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{3}} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$
